# Systematic organizational reviews: what conclusions survive differences in designs and outcomes?

Methodological review draft (v2, full-text appraised) · not submission-ready · 9 October 2026

## Review question

How do systematic reviews communicate uncertainty when included organizational studies differ in intervention, outcome and design?

Focus confirmed by the author on 9 October 2026 ([decisions](question-decisions.md)). Written as a methodological review with a meta-research protocol.

## Evidence base and method

The author's reference folder (`Paper 21 Dec 2024/References`) holds 24 PDFs. Twenty-three were identified against Crossref, and none is retracted. Two were excluded: a conceptual research agenda and an encyclopedia entry. The remaining **22 systematic or scoping reviews** (3 with meta-analysis; 2 combined with bibliometrics) form the audit sample. They span HRM, OB, health-professions education, management education and sustainability.

Each review was searched in full text for eleven reporting elements (`elements.py`). For the five elements that bear directly on uncertainty (quality appraisal, heterogeneity, certainty of evidence, double screening and registration), every machine hit was judged by hand (`verdicts.py`). Eight hits were false positives, for example "formative evaluation" matching "quality", or "regional heterogeneity" referring to policy rather than to included studies. The other six elements are reported as machine-detected counts and may include false positives.

## Findings

### Uncertainty-relevant practices are the exception

| Element | Reviews (of 22) | Basis |
|---|---:|---|
| Quality or risk-of-bias appraisal of included studies | 4 | hand-verified [R1, R2, R3, R4] |
| Certainty or strength of the evidence stated | 3 | hand-verified [R2, R3, R4] |
| Heterogeneity or inconsistency across included studies discussed | 5 | hand-verified [R4, R5, R6, R7, R8] |
| Screening or coding by two or more reviewers | 7 | hand-verified [R1, R2, R3, R4, R9, R6, R10] |
| Protocol registered (PROSPERO) | 2 | hand-verified [R2, R3] |
| Databases named | 22 | machine-detected |
| Search terms or strategy described | 22 | machine-detected (broad match) |
| Eligibility criteria stated | 18 | machine-detected |
| Synthesis method named | 18 | machine-detected |
| PRISMA or flow diagram | 12 | machine-detected |

The pattern is consistent. Nearly every review reports *how it found* studies: databases, terms and eligibility. Few report *how much confidence* the reader should place in what was found. Only 4 of 22 appraised the quality of included studies, and only 3 said anything about the strength or certainty of the overall evidence.

### What good practice looks like in this collection

The two PROSPERO-registered reviews from the same research group show the full chain. One rated strength of evidence on design limitations, indirectness, "unexplained heterogeneity or inconsistency of results", imprecision and publication bias [R2, PDF p8]. The other built evidence categories "from the GRADE approach ... for quantitative studies ... and the CERQual approach for qualitative studies" [R3, PDF p9]. It also reported reviewer agreement: "Cohen’s Kappa ratings for both sifts represented good levels of agreement between reviewers (range 0.74– 0.86)" [R3, PDF p8].

A smaller review tied its conclusion to design directly: "All studies were based in cross-sectional designs, which detracted from the overall quality of evidence" [R4, PDF p15]. It stated plainly that the central association "showed inconsistent results" [R4, PDF p14]. Another identified measurement as the source of non-comparability: "The widespread heterogeneity in operationalizations of team satisfaction is likely to affect the comparability of studies and results" [R5, PDF p8].

These are the statements the review question asks about. They tell readers which conclusions depend on design and measurement differences.

### How the others communicate (or do not)

The remaining reviews mostly report descriptive maps: counts by year, country, theory and method, followed by thematic frameworks or research agendas. Where they mention disagreement among studies, it is as a substantive finding ("mixed results") [R6, R7, R8], not as a limit on what the review can conclude. No review outside the quality-appraising four graded its conclusions by design strength. Mixed findings were not routinely traced to differences in samples, measures or designs.

## Conclusions this collection supports

1. **Uncertainty is rarely communicated systematically.** Search transparency is high; appraisal and certainty statements are rare (4 and 3 of 22).
2. **Heterogeneity tends to be reported as content, not as a constraint.** "Mixed findings" appear as results but seldom limit the review's conclusions.
3. **Workable tools already exist and are used in this collection.** GRADE and CERQual style strength ratings [R2, R3] and a plain design-based caveat [R4] show the options range from full grading to a single honest sentence.
4. A minimal standard for organizational reviews would require at least one of these, plus an explicit link from each headline conclusion to the designs that support it.

## Limits

- 22 reviews from one curated folder, several outside OB (health information systems, ecotourism). The audit illustrates practices; it does not estimate field-wide rates.
- Six elements are machine-detected only and probably overcount; "search strategy described" in particular matched broadly.
- Online supplements were not searched.

## Proposed research direction (meta-research)

The companion protocol samples systematic reviews from named OB/HRM journals over a fixed window. It codes the five uncertainty elements above with two independent coders. Its outcome is the share of review conclusions qualified by design or certainty, and whether registration or reporting-guideline use predicts such qualification. No participant data are collected.

# Paper 21 — Meta-research protocol v2: Uncertainty communication in systematic reviews

> **Status: PROPOSAL.** Unit of analysis = published articles; no human participants. No coding has been done and no prevalence results exist. Version 2 replaces `paper-21-dec-2024-protocol.md`.

## 1. Question
How often do systematic reviews in named OB/HRM journals over a fixed window report each of the practices below, and does reporting change over the window?

## 2. Sampling frame
- **Frame:** systematic reviews in named OB/HRM journals over a fixed window. The journal list and the 5-year window are fixed in the OSF pre-registration **before** searching.
- **Retrieval:** Scopus/OpenAlex query by journal ISSN and window (query string archived); every record de-duplicated by DOI.
- **Eligibility:** screened by title/abstract, then full text, by two independent screeners; disagreements resolved by discussion; PRISMA-style flow reported.
- **Sample size:** to estimate a reporting prevalence within ±.08 (95% CI, worst case p = .50) requires **151 eligible articles**. If more are eligible, a random sample of 151 (seed archived) is coded; if fewer, all are coded and the achieved precision reported.

## 3. Coding manual (core items)
| Code | Values | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| quality / risk-of-bias appraisal | present / absent / unclear | definition and decision rules in the coding manual (pilot on 15 articles) |
| certainty grading | present / absent / unclear | definition and decision rules in the coding manual (pilot on 15 articles) |
| heterogeneity linked to conclusions | present / absent / unclear | definition and decision rules in the coding manual (pilot on 15 articles) |
| double screening | present / absent / unclear | definition and decision rules in the coding manual (pilot on 15 articles) |
| registration | present / absent / unclear | definition and decision rules in the coding manual (pilot on 15 articles) |

Plus descriptors: journal, year, country of data, design, sample size.

## 4. Reliability
Two coders code **83 articles** independently (≥ 20% of the sample and ≥ 83, the number needed to show κ > .60 when true κ = .80, one-sided α = .05, 80% power). Codes below κ = .60 are revised and re-coded. The remainder is single-coded with 10% spot checks.

## 5. Analysis
Prevalence with Wilson 95% CIs per code; logistic regression of each code on publication year (trend) and design; all counts are reproducible from the archived coding sheet.

## 6. Ethics
Published literature only — no human participants. An IEC **exemption** request (ICMR 2017: research on publicly available information) is filed with the AMET IEC for the record.

## 7. Open science
Pre-registration, search strings, coding manual, coding sheet and analysis script on OSF.

## 8. Readiness checklist
- [ ] Journal list and window fixed
- [ ] Coding manual piloted (15 articles) and revised
- [ ] Second coder identified
- [ ] OSF pre-registration (link: ________)
- [ ] IEC exemption letter (reference: ________)
